newsitem.title: CHINA: World parliamentarians' conference opens in China.
newsitem.headline: World parliamentarians' conference opens in China.

text.p: An international meeting of parliamentarians opened in China on Monday with calls for greater protection of human rights worldwide and the dismissal of an Iraqi appeal for solidarity against the United States.
Delegates at the opening session of the 96th conference of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) voted down an emergency proposal from Baghdad to debate recent U.S. attacks on Iraq.
At an earlier opening ceremony in Beijing's cavernous Great Hall of the People, IPU leaders had said the conference would focus on discussion of human rights and food issues.
"The right to food is the right to life itself... Without securing the right to life no other human right will hold any significance," IPU president Ahmed Fathy Sorour told delegates.
"I am confident that your deliberations will focus on a detailed plan of action containing feasible and concrete proposals that all states should be committed to carry out," he said.

Delegates to the conference, a talking shop that will allow formal and informal discussions among 633 members of parliament from 120 nations, should try to find ways to guarantee food in an age of increasing globalisation, he said.
During the opening session, the conference voted to also hold a debate sponsored by Canada and Germany on mine-clearance and a worldwide ban on anti-personnel mines.
Any resolution from the debate will be non-binding.
U.S. cruise missile attacks on southern Iraq in early September provoked an impassioned appeal from the Iraqi delegation for an emergency debate.
"All countries in the world should express their solidarity," the Iraqi spokesman said. "I wish to make an appeal -- please side with Iraq."
The proposal, which required an 80 percent vote in its favour to proceed, failed to gain a majority and was dropped.
The five-day IPU meeting will be the first time China has permitted open debate on human rights by foreigners since the U.N.-sponsored World Conference on Women in Beijing last year.
China rejects most foreign criticism of its human rights record as interference in its internal affairs and routinely refuses visas to rights groups it considers hostile.
At the opening ceremony, United Nations ambassador Joseph Reed appealed for support from parliamentarians in the U.N. battle for funding and political support.
Reed pointedly thanked China for paying its U.N. dues on time and mourned the United States' reluctance to do likewise.

"The United Nations is still facing the worst and most protracted financial crisis in its history. As of 31 August, arrears in payment for the regular and peace-keeping budgets amounted to almost $3.0 billion," he said.
"I appeal to you, parliamentarians of the world, to continue to give us the support we need," he said.
